title: Unity VFX Entirely by AI (6.2 Astra) - FireAttackV1
author: KorvinNasa13
selftext:
Here’s my previous post: [Link (Knockback VFX)](https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1y27y8a/unity_vfx_entirely_by_ai_62_astra_knockback/)

This is probably the toughest effect I’ve tried to make with AI and custom skills so far. It’s still pretty rough, but overall I think it looks okay.

It definitely still needs that human touch, but that’s kind of the whole point. I didn’t touch anything by hand here, it’s just raw AI + my feedback/comments. This is the result after the 6 iterations.

comments.author: lazershunpo

replies.author: KorvinNasa13
replies.body:
Long story short, at this stage I'm finding random VFX online and trying to get AI to recreate them without any manual intervention on my end. I'm just providing guidance, pointing out issues with the flow, and eventually documenting everything it learns in the skills.

This is only the first phase. Once I've built up a solid foundation of effects (or rather, once all that knowledge is reflected in the skills and AI has a better understanding of motion, anticipation, charge, color theory, etc.), I'll start giving it loosely defined prompts + sketches and see how it builds effects based on that information.

Since I'm a Technical/VFX Artist myself, I can guide AI and point out which elements of an effect could be improved, teach it how to recognize patterns and break effects down into individual components.

Obviously, I can't change the model's architecture or weights, so these skills essentially form a kind of guidebook. They're designed to be effect-agnostic, meaning their main purpose is to generalize the process of creating VFX so that AI can identify what's important and correctly combine everything to create any type of effect.

Essentially, skills are additional context and the more relevant, high-quality and compact that context is, the better the effects turn out (at least that's what I've observed so far).

Also, just to be clear, the original reference is NOT my VFX. I'm not 100% sure whether mentioning the artists by name could be considered promotion. Every community has its own rules and sometimes they can be pretty strict, but here's the creator of this particular effect: [HKRealTimeVFX](https://www.youtube.com/@HKRealTimeVFX).

The way I see it, most effects are built around certain patterns and follow pretty much the same rules. You can change textures, colors, add some cosmetic elements, but the underlying principles remain the same.

So when I look at an effect, I can mentally break it down, understand what it's made of and how to rebuild it. That's my main goal right now. It's not even so much about motion or anything else, but rather about teaching AI how all these individual elements fit together.

In addition to that, I've been "teaching" AI using my own effects, breaking them down and explaining how they work. I've also been feeding it CC0 articles and various educational materials to help it better understand certain concepts. I went through a basic set of shaders, optimization techniques, meshes and noise textures (most VFX are essentially just combinations of different noise/mask textures and shaders🤣) and showed it how individual elements are created.

replies.author: KorvinNasa13
replies.body:
Thanks! Pretty much, but before that I also did some "pre-training" using my own effects, purchased assets and CC0 articles.

I also point out mistakes and explain how to do things correctly (during iterations) and which techniques to use to achieve the desired result.

But yeah, the current plan is to build up a solid base of effects and then run more in-depth tests in completely clean projects with NO existing assets.

Right now, I'm using a project that already contains some assets (that I built myself + some purchased), so AI can refer to them, even though it creates everything from scratch.

replies.author: KorvinNasa13
replies.body:
Everything I'm writing below is based purely on my own experience and may not reflect other people's experiences, but this is how I see it.

**Regarding copying:**

I wish it were that easy and AI was actually great at "just copying stuff" out of the box.

Here's another example. I've spent a lot of time creating UI, including for large-scale mobile projects with millions of users. So when I started building my own personal project, I created a foundation for the UI (in Unity), including complex screens, and then asked AI to build additional screens so I wouldn't have to create them manually. More specifically, I asked it to copy my techniques and build new screens based on them.

And what did AI end up doing? Something that wasn't even remotely close to production-ready UI or what I already had in my project, even though I specifically asked it to follow my existing pipeline and refer to my examples.

UI-heavy projects can suffer from pretty severe freezes when opening or interacting with UI. In my case, around 60% of the game consists of UI, with complex adaptive UI elements that can expand and resize their parents and even their parents' parents, with the entire UI in motion.

There are a lot of things to consider here. Avoiding excessive material instances and unnecessary GC, moving dynamic elements to separate Canvases to avoid expensive Canvas rebuilds, dealing with the fact that MaterialPropertyBlock doesn't work with uGUI and figuring out how to combine elements without creating unnecessary material instances.

Maybe a more complex shader? Maybe swapping materials? How to properly use atlases? How to pack elements into atlases without wasting memory? How to properly use Layout Groups? A lot of people still use Content Size Fitters on elements whose RectTransforms are already being driven by other components, resulting in conflicting updates, elements getting stuck and incorrect position updates.

I had to literally sit down and explain to AI how to work with UI in this specific project, how to use the UI prefabs I'd created, how to optimize things and where to look whenever it had questions (pointing it to my own examples).

And now I can just show it an image, explain the motion and purpose of the elements and it recreates everything almost 1:1, including complex screens with transitions and animations. If I showed this to someone, they probably WOULDN'T believe it, because these UI elements are genuinely complex. I'm not talking about a single window, but something like 10 different windows with scroll views, transitions, and animations. I just show it one image, explain what happens when you click here or there and that's it.

Pure magic if you ask me. Especially since for the longest time I thought skills were just a gimmick or a placebo and many ppl actually recommended NOT using them at all or periodically removing them to give the model more freedom. I'm not falling for that again😁

It was far from easy to get AI to simply "copy stuff" based on what I'd originally shown it. I had to explain WHAT was being done in the project and WHY. It took a lot of iterations, but the result was worth it.

**Regarding originality:**

My current goal is different and I've more or less explained it in the other comments here.

But as I've already mentioned, I've worked and still work as a VFX Artist, and throughout all these years, I've rarely seen anything truly original or unique. To me, something original or unique is something I've RARELY seen before. As the saying goes "Everything new is just the well-forgotten old."

There have been plenty of times when I've looked at a project made in Unity/Unreal, seen its effects and immediately recognized which asset pack they came from. Or when I'm looking at other artists effects on ArtStation/Elsewhere, I can already see who they might have been inspired by.

At work, I've been asked countless times to make something like "that effect from another popular game, but make it slightly different so it's not obvious." Meanwhile, that popular game had already taken inspiration from another game, and the cycle continues 🤣

And quite often, you could create an entirely new effect simply by combining elements from 2–3 existing effects and changing their colors/textures and people wouldn't even notice. I can also open the Asset Store and see that most effects are essentially variations of other effects.

But, once I'm done with the first phase, I'll start trying to create "original" effects using AI, based on prompts + sketches.
